name: Sara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What was on your desk before lunch?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara Evans, fifty-eight, and I prepare home-care agency accounts and tax returns at an accounting firm. A signed visit sheet showed a carer had been entered twice this morning; I like fixing that before it changes her pay. I dislike closing the month from an unsigned log. I'm an experienced mid-level accountant of average skill, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do tools and home life fit together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day to group visit logs and check the totals against signed sheets. My partner Jules does irregular home-repair jobs, our children are grown and pay their own bills, and we still have a small mortgage. My accounting pay is low, we have less than one month saved, and few similar firms are nearby. I try a new tool early, but a funded shift is more useful than a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still close the home-care agency accounts and prepare tax returns at month end. I use AI every day to group visit logs by client, then match its totals to the signed time sheets before a senior reviews the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agencies a worker's signed visit time has to agree with the bill. I'd tell my team that a tidy AI list is only the first check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fifty-eight, experienced at this mid-level work and about average for the firm, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. My pay is still low for the job. My partner Jules and I have less than one month of expenses saved and few similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing agency accounts and returns with the AI grouping I already use. Next month I'd cancel a second television package we rarely watch and move its twenty-five monthly charge to an emergency account. I'd check that the first transfer arrives before promising ourselves a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our bills even if work stays familiar. A signed care visit can be checked; our emergency account still needs money in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household bill had to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules does part-time home repairs, and the calls are uneven. Our grown son and daughter pay their own bills, while we still have a small mortgage. Last week the car needed tyres and the boiler needed a service, and we could not pay both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the duplicate visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A care worker's visit time was entered twice yesterday, so I checked the signed sheet and called the agency manager. I like finding a mistake before it changes a worker's pay. I dislike being asked to close the month with an unsigned visit log.

say: I would match **signed visit sheets** to agency bills.
I would use **AI groupings** only as the first check.
think: Our **mortgage and repair bills** already stretch low pay.
My **mid-level experience** does not create an emergency reserve.
do: Continue **care-agency accounts** with daily AI grouping and senior review.
Cancel the **extra television package** and save twenty-five monthly.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing bill pressure.
S0.quote: A signed care visit can be checked; our emergency account still needs money in it.
fieldNote: Her **average mid-level skill** and professional qualification coexist with lower pay and a sub-month reserve.
Her **daily AI grouping** is an existing routine; the unused television package funds an actual monthly savings transfer.

steps.text: Keep care-agency accounts with daily AI grouping and signed visit checks
Cancel second television package and transfer twenty-five monthly to emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could draft agency replies and check most visit logs, which are hours our firm bills for now. Someone still has to ask whether a carer actually attended when the log and invoice differ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to show our paid review rota before changing it. I'd tell agency clients that an automated list needs an accountable person when a worker's pay is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own review day could be cut if the agencies pay less. Jules's repair calls are too uneven to cover the mortgage and bills by themselves, and our reserve lasts weeks. I use AI every day, but I cannot turn software speed into a paid position without the firm's decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a new AI-assisted exception checklist from approved visit data during paid hours and have the senior test the first twenty cases. I'd ask the partner for a written paid hour each week to handle the exceptions; if refused, I'd keep the present paid review rota while offered and the current signed-sheet check. If my hours are cut, I'd apply only to posted paid care-agency coordinator jobs with written pay covering our mortgage and bills, a signed start and hours fitting Jules's confirmed repair bookings; if none fits, I'd keep any paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my wage. A good exception list cannot pay the mortgage without a funded hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would the checklist catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker called last week because a missed visit on the screen had removed part of her pay. The signed sheet showed she had attended, so the agency corrected the invoice. I want the checklist to flag that before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a coordinator shift fit home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules drives to repair calls early on some days, and I use our car on the others. A new coordinator role would need an actual shift start and transport plan. I would compare the written hours with Jules's booked jobs before accepting.

I would keep a **person accountable** for worker-pay errors.
think: My **review day** could be cut when agencies pay less for checked visits.
Jules’s **variable calls** cannot cover our mortgage alone.
do: Test a **new exception checklist** on approved paid data with senior checks.
Seek a **written paid hour** weekly; otherwise keep signed-sheet reviews.
Compare **posted work hours** with Jules’s booked repairs and shared car after cuts; apply only with written mortgage-and-bills pay and signed start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost pay.
S1.quote: A good exception list cannot pay the mortgage without a funded hour.
fieldNote: The **new AI checklist** is a distinct paid workflow, tested on twenty approved cases with senior review.
A **coordinator move** needs posted funding, written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and transport fitting Jules’s confirmed bookings.

steps.text: Test new AI checklist on twenty approved paid cases with senior review
Seek written approval for one paid weekly exception hour
Keep offered paid signed-sheet reviews if new weekly hour refused
Apply after cuts: posted care-coordinator work, written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start, shared car fitting Jules’s bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare and check the agency accounts and tax returns I spend most days on. Robots around 2031 come later, but the desk can lose its fee first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for written notice and funded work with clients before anyone is cut. I'd tell Jules we should protect the mortgage payment before ordering new furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my accounting post could end in the first year after 2028. We have less than a month saved and Jules's repair wages vary, so a lost payslip would hit us quickly. I do not know what pension income I would get or when, so I will ask for a statement rather than assume it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the one-time five-hundred dining table order and hold that cash for the mortgage. While still employed, I'd check posted home-care coordinator vacancies that include real in-person visits; scheduling and records themselves face AGI too. If the firm ends my post in the first year after 2028, I'd claim income help only if eligible and take a funded care role only with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting Jules's confirmed repair bookings and our shared car; if none fits, I'd take only paid firm files still offered and keep searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. We cannot feed the mortgage an annual forecast while a payslip is missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I would tell our grown children we're delaying the table, not asking them to pay for it. We would write down which repair calls are actually booked before comparing a care job's rota. A verbal offer cannot keep the car in two places at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a care coordinator be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home-care office could post a job, but much of its planning is also screen work. I'd ask how many hours are real home visits, which robots may affect around 2031. I would not resign until the wage and start are written.

I would protect the **mortgage cash** before furniture.
think: My **accounts post** may end in the first year after 2028.
Our **sub-month reserve** cannot bridge a lost wage.
do: Postpone the **one-time table order** and hold five hundred.
Check **posted care coordinator roles** with real in-person visits while still paid.
Take **funded care work** after 2028 loss only with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and shared-car hours fitting Jules’s confirmed bookings.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected pay loss.
S2.quote: We cannot feed the mortgage an annual forecast while a payslip is missing.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches both accountant work and care scheduling in 2028; physical home visits may persist until later robots.
The **funded care role** needs written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and a rota aligned with booked repairs and the shared car.

steps.text: Postpone one-time dining table order and hold five hundred for mortgage

Move after loss with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start, shared car fitting Jules’s bookings.
Claim eligible income help and take offered paid firm files if no role fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me test in-person care visits while my accounting desk is still paid. AGI in 2031 would still take tax preparation and scheduling, and robots around 2034 might later affect home visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm for paid release and a home-care client for supervised paid visits. I'd tell my family I need to know what the work is like before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the agency's figures, not how to support a person safely in their home. Our reserve is too thin for unpaid training. Jules's repair income cannot replace my accounting wage while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd ask a care agency for three supervised paid home-visit shifts and my firm for paid release, then work them only if both approve in writing. If either refuses, I'd keep my paid accounts rota while offered and ask another agency for a funded place. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if tax work ends, I'd take a posted funded care coordinator role only with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting Jules's confirmed repair bookings and our shared car; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take any paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a desk loss, but supervised visits are something I can test. A balance sheet cannot tell me whether I can help a client out of bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you decline the invitation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A care manager invited me to observe a morning visit last month, but it was unpaid and I declined. I would want a supervisor and a paid shift before taking responsibility. An invitation is not training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the agency refuses pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency offers only unpaid shadowing, I will keep the accounting wage and ask elsewhere. A paid supervised shift would show whether I can do the physical work. I would not assume a care vacancy exists just because a manager likes me.

I would request **firm paid release** before trying them.

Keep **offered paid accounts** if either approval fails.
Seek **funded care work** after 2031 loss only with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and shared car fitting Jules’s booked repairs.
feel: I feel **anxious** while testing real care work.
S3.quote: A balance sheet cannot tell me whether I can help a client out of bed.
fieldNote: The **three-visit trial** needs agency wages, a supervisor and written firm-paid release, not an unpaid invitation.
A **post-2031 move** needs a posted funded role, written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and Jules-compatible car rota.

steps.text: Work three supervised home visits only with agency pay and written firm-paid release
Keep offered paid accounts if agency or firm refuses trial funding
Take posted care role after loss: written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start, shared car fitting Jules’s bookings.
Claim eligible help and take offered firm work if no funded care role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might let me gain real care experience before AGI reaches my tax work in 2036. Robots around 2039 could then reach parts of hands-on care, though people may still want a person beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the agency and firm to put paid training and real vacancies in writing. I'd tell our grown children that their wages are for their homes, not ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I might have a pension, but I do not know its payable amount or date. Our mortgage and less than a month saved today make the long runway feel narrow. I will not stop work on an age alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a pension statement each January and compare any payable amount with our mortgage and bills while keeping paid accounts work if offered. Next spring I'd take three supervised paid care shifts only with agency pay and written firm paid release; if refused, I'd stay on the paid accounts rota while it exists. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax post ends and pension income is insufficient or not payable, I'd take a posted funded care role only with written mortgage-and-bills pay, signed start and hours fitting Jules's confirmed bookings and our car; if none fits, I'd claim eligible help and take only paid firm hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present cash despite the ten-year runway. Ten years of planning is not a pension payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would adult children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I would look at the statement at the kitchen table. If a real pension covers the bills, we can decide separately whether to stop then. We will not count our son's or daughter's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you open a care business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency has no paid role, I would look at other posted care jobs before leaving the firm. I would not buy a private care business with our tiny reserve. I need actual wages and a start date.

feel: I feel **anxious** about present cash pressure.
S4.quote: Ten years of planning is not a pension payment.
fieldNote: At **sixty-eight in 2036**, pension eligibility and adequacy remain unverified until an actual statement arrives.
The **care transition** requires agency-paid supervised shifts and firm-paid release; a later funded role needs written pay, start and car hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because agency accounts are desk work and our mortgage reserve is under a month. Jules's repair calls are not regular enough to cover a lost accounting wage. Written notice, a funded care role and paid supervised visits would help. A signed visit sheet can fix wages; it cannot replace mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the care client wants someone to explain a corrected visit log in person. I can do the figures now and would need training before the home visit. The agency has to pay for both kinds of time.

headlineQuote: A signed visit sheet can fix wages; it cannot replace mine.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Sara prepares home-care agency accounts and returns as an experienced mid-level accountant.
Her **bachelor’s and professional qualification** accompany average skill, not junior standing.
She uses **AI daily** to group visits but checks signed time sheets.
Jules’s **variable repair work**, grown children, mortgage and sub-month savings keep money tight.
Low **accounting pay** and few nearby firms make funded care work a conditional alternative.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her desk wage before a mortgage month is saved.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, funded care work and paid supervised visits.
